newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin visits Kremlin, foes plan new attack.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin visits Kremlin, foes plan new attack.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin, keeping up a steady workload as he recovers from pneumonia, met Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov in the Kremlin on Thursday as his political foes prepared a fresh attack.
Kulikov said Yeltsin, who is still convalescing from his illness at a country residence outside Moscow, was in "good working form" during their 40-minute meeting.
Brief television footage showed a dark-suited Yeltsin, looking thin but smiling and moving easily, greeting the uniformed Kulikov at his Kremlin office.
The State Duma lower house of parliament, which is dominated by communists and nationalists, is due to discuss a resolution on Friday calling on Yeltsin to quit on health grounds.
The resolution has no legal force but it will force Yeltsin to demonstrate that his health problems do not prevent him running the country.

Efforts to crack down on crime will be part of this strategy and Interfax news agency quoted Kulikov as saying Yeltsin had given him "carte blanche" to deal with economic crime, which costs Russia's state coffers billions of dollars every year.
The two men also discussed measures to improve the work of the Interior Ministry, the customs service and the tax police.
"The main thing, in the president's view, is strengthening fiscal and customs discipline with decisive actions," the presidential press service said in a statement released after the meeting.
Yeltsin appointed the conservative Kulikov a deputy prime minister on Monday, giving him responsibility for coordinating the fight against organised crime.
The government often blames tax dodgers -- companies and individuals -- for chronic delays in paying wages and pensions.
Yeltsin's press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky told Interfax that pensions would be a major topic of a radio address Yeltsin plans to make to the nation on Friday,
He said Yeltsin was angry at suggestions made recently by the head of the Russian Pension Fund, Vassily Barchuk, that working pensioners could forfeit their right to a pension.
Yeltsin's radio address, to be broadcast at 11 a.m. (0800 GMT), will also touch on Moscow's relations with breakaway Chechnya and on the possibility of constitutional reform, Yastrzhembsky added.
Former rebel guerrilla leader Aslan Maskhadov formally took office as Chechnya's first post-war president on Wednesday, vowing to pursue his aim of full independence from Moscow.
Russian news agencies said Maskhadov started forming a governent on Thursday.
Moscow, whose military bid to quash the rebels ended in humiliation, still hopes to use economic inducements to persuade Chechnya to remain within the Russian Federation.
Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin would also reply to critics in the State Duma lower house of parliament who want to water down his presidential powers.
"(The critics) must learn to work with the constitution," he quoted the president as saying.
Yegor Stroyev, chairman of Russia's upper house Federation Council said on Thursday Yeltsin that would make his annual address to both chambers of parliament on March 5.

Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov said this week that Yeltsin's performance before deputies, along with a planned summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton later in March, would reveal his real ability to rule Russia.
"The president continues to be incapacitated...everything is falling to pieces in front of our eyes," Zyuganov said.
